question: Which of the following is a vector quantity?
What is the weight of a 5 kg object on Earth? (g = 10 N/kg)
A car travels at a constant speed on a straight road. What can we conclude about the forces acting on it?
options: There are no forces acting on it
The driving force is greater than friction
The resultant force is in the direction of motion

question: A resultant force of 30 N acts on a 6 kg object. What is its acceleration?
A spring has a spring constant of 40 N/m. What force is needed to extend it by 0.25 m?
What does the gradient of a distance-time graph represent?
What does the area under a velocity-time graph represent?
Which of the following would increase the braking distance of a car?
A 2 kg ball moves at 5 m/s. What is its momentum?
Newton's Third Law states that forces act in pairs. Which statement correctly describes these pairs?
options: Both forces act on the same object in opposite directions
The forces act on different objects and are equal and opposite
One force is always larger than the other
The forces only act when objects are in contact
correct: The forces act on different objects and are equal and opposite

question: A force of 25 N moves an object 4 m in the direction of the force. How much work is done?
What is elastic deformation?
options: When an object stretches and does not return to its original shape
When an object returns to its original shape after the force is removed
When an object breaks under a large force
correct: When an object returns to its original shape after the force is removed

question: Which of the following affects thinking distance?
Two objects collide and stick together. Which law applies to this collision?
A car travels 100 m north then 60 m south. What is its displacement?
Newton's Second Law states that force = mass × __________.
Weight = mass × gravitational field __________.
Hooke's Law states that extension is proportional to force, provided the __________ limit is not exceeded.
Momentum = mass × __________.
Stopping distance = thinking distance + __________ distance.
The gradient of a velocity-time graph gives the __________.
Work done = __________ × distance.
Speed is a __________ quantity, while velocity is a vector quantity.
An object's tendency to resist changes in motion is called __________.
The total momentum before a collision equals the total after — this is the law of conservation of __________.
Match each quantity to whether it is a scalar or vector.
Match each Newton's Law to its correct statement.

pairs.definition: An object stays at rest or moves at constant velocity unless a resultant force acts
Every action has an equal and opposite reaction on a different object

question: Match each graph description to what it tells us about motion.
Match each factor to whether it affects thinking distance or braking distance.
Match each force to whether it is a contact or non-contact force.

pairs.definition: Contact force — objects must be touching
Non-contact force — acts at a distance
Contact force — objects must be touching
Non-contact force — acts at a distance

question: State Newton's First Law of motion.
mark_scheme: An object remains at rest or continues at constant velocity (1); unless acted on by a resultant force (1) — accept either.

question: Calculate the weight of a 70 kg person on Earth. (g = 10 N/kg)
State what Hooke's Law tells us about a spring.
mark_scheme: Extension is directly proportional to force applied (1); provided elastic limit is not exceeded (1) — accept either.

question: Calculate the momentum of a 1500 kg car travelling at 20 m/s.
Explain why a tired driver has a longer stopping distance than an alert driver.
mark_scheme: A tired driver has a slower reaction time (1); thinking distance increases (1); overall stopping distance is longer (1) — any two.

question: Describe how you would investigate Hooke's Law using a spring in the laboratory.
mark_scheme: Hang known masses on the spring and measure the extension (1); plot a graph of force against extension (1); straight line through origin shows F proportional to extension (1); identify elastic limit where graph curves (1) — any two.

question: A skydiver reaches terminal velocity. Explain what this means in terms of forces.
mark_scheme: At terminal velocity the resultant force is zero (1); weight downwards equals air resistance upwards (1); no resultant force so no acceleration (1) — any two.

question: A car accelerates from 10 m/s to 30 m/s in 5 seconds. Calculate its acceleration.
Explain, using Newton's Third Law, what happens when a rocket expels gas downwards.
mark_scheme: The rocket pushes gas downwards (1); by Newton's Third Law the gas pushes the rocket upwards with an equal and opposite force (1).

question: Explain why crumple zones in cars reduce the risk of injury in a collision.
mark_scheme: Crumple zones increase the time taken for the car to stop (1); impulse = force × time = change in momentum (1); same change in momentum over longer time means smaller force (1); smaller force means less injury to passengers (1) — any three.

question: Describe the motion of an object from a velocity-time graph that shows: a positive gradient, then a horizontal line, then a negative gradient.
mark_scheme: Positive gradient: object accelerating (1); horizontal line: object moving at constant velocity (1); negative gradient: object decelerating (1); if line reaches zero the object has stopped (1) — any three.

question: Explain the difference between mass and weight, and describe how they would differ on the Moon compared to Earth.
mark_scheme: Mass is the amount of matter in an object — measured in kg (1); weight is the gravitational force acting on it — measured in N (1); mass stays the same on the Moon (1); weight is less on the Moon because gravitational field strength is lower (1) — any three.

question: A car of mass 1200 kg accelerates from rest to 24 m/s in 8 seconds. Calculate the resultant force and explain what happens to the acceleration if the driving force stays the same but the car gains passengers.
mark_scheme: a = (24 - 0) / 8 = 3 m/s² (1); F = ma = 1200 × 3 = 3600 N (1); more passengers increases total mass (1); same force on larger mass gives smaller acceleration (1).

question: Evaluate the factors that affect the stopping distance of a vehicle travelling at high speed on a wet road at night.
mark_scheme: High speed increases both thinking and braking distance (1); wet road reduces friction increasing braking distance (1); night driving may cause tiredness increasing reaction time (1); poor visibility means hazard seen later (1); worn tyres would further increase braking distance (1) — any four.

question: A 3 kg ball moving at 6 m/s collides with a stationary 2 kg ball. After the collision they move together. Calculate their combined velocity after the collision.
mark_scheme: Total momentum before = 3 × 6 + 2 × 0 = 18 kg m/s (1); conservation of momentum: total after = 18 kg m/s (1); (3 + 2) × v = 18 (1); v = 18 ÷ 5 = 3.6 m/s (1).

question: A student plots a force-extension graph for a spring and finds the line curves after a certain point. Explain what this shows and calculate the spring constant for the linear section if a force of 8 N causes an extension of 0.04 m.
mark_scheme: Straight line shows Hooke's Law is obeyed (1); curve shows elastic limit exceeded (1); beyond elastic limit inelastic deformation occurs (1); k = F/e = 8 ÷ 0.04 = 200 N/m (1).

question: Describe and explain the motion of a skydiver from leaving the plane to landing safely, referring to forces and velocity throughout.
mark_scheme: Weight greater than air resistance so accelerates downward (1); as speed increases air resistance increases (1); eventually air resistance equals weight — terminal velocity (1); parachute opens: air resistance greatly increases (1); resultant force upward so decelerates (1); new lower terminal velocity reached (1); lands safely (1) — any five.

question: Evaluate the safety features in modern cars that reduce the risk of injury in a collision. Refer to momentum, impulse and force in your answer.
mark_scheme: In a collision momentum changes rapidly (1); impulse = force × time = change in momentum (1); to reduce force, time must increase (1); crumple zones increase collision time reducing force (1); seatbelts stretch increasing deceleration time (1); airbags cushion impact (1); headrests prevent whiplash (1) — any six.

question: A rocket launches from Earth. Explain, using all three of Newton's Laws, how the rocket accelerates, reaches constant velocity, and how it could decelerate.
mark_scheme: First Law: rocket stays still until thrust acts (1); Second Law: thrust greater than weight so resultant force causes acceleration F = ma (1); as fuel burns rocket lighter so acceleration increases (1); Third Law: rocket expels gas down, gas pushes rocket up with equal and opposite force (1); air resistance increases with speed — eventually equals thrust giving constant velocity (1); to decelerate, thrust reduced so resultant force opposes motion (1) — any six.

question: A footballer kicks a ball with a force of 40 N at 30° above the horizontal. Explain the difference between a scalar and a vector quantity, and explain why force is a vector. State the horizontal and vertical components of the kick (sin 30° = 0.5, cos 30° = 0.87).
mark_scheme: Scalar: magnitude only, no direction (1); vector: has both magnitude and direction (1); force is a vector because it has both size and direction (1); horizontal component = 40 × 0.87 = 34.8 N; vertical component = 40 × 0.5 = 20 N (1 for both correct).

question: A cyclist travels at 12 m/s and brakes uniformly to rest in 6 seconds. Calculate the deceleration of the cyclist and the distance travelled during braking.
mark_scheme: a = (v − u) / t = (0 − 12) / 6 = −2 m/s² (1); deceleration = 2 m/s² (1); distance = area under v-t graph = ½ × 12 × 6 (1); distance = 36 m (1).

question: Explain the difference between contact and non-contact forces. Give two examples of each and describe how the resultant force is calculated when two forces act in the same direction and in opposite directions along a straight line.
mark_scheme: Contact forces require objects to be touching, e.g. friction, tension, normal reaction (any two) (1); non-contact forces act at a distance, e.g. gravity, magnetic force, electrostatic force (any two) (1); forces in same direction: add them together (1); forces in opposite directions: subtract the smaller from the larger; direction is that of the larger force (1).

question: A spring of spring constant 250 N/m is stretched by a force of 15 N. Calculate the extension of the spring and the elastic potential energy stored. (Ee = ½ ke²)

Explain how Newton's Second Law applies to an aircraft taking off. The aircraft has a mass of 50 000 kg and engines provide a total thrust of 600 000 N. Friction and drag total 100 000 N. Calculate the acceleration.
Describe what a distance-time graph and a velocity-time graph each tell us about motion. For each type of graph, explain what a straight line and a curved line indicate.
mark_scheme: Distance-time graph: gradient = speed (1); straight line = constant speed; curve = changing speed (acceleration or deceleration) (1); velocity-time graph: gradient = acceleration; area under graph = distance travelled (1); straight line = constant acceleration; curve = changing acceleration (1).

question: A person of mass 60 kg climbs stairs of vertical height 4 m. Calculate the work done against gravity and explain why the actual energy used by the person is greater than this value. (g = 10 N/kg)
mark_scheme: Weight = mg = 60 × 10 = 600 N (1); work done = force × distance = 600 × 4 = 2400 J (1); actual energy used is greater because the body is not 100% efficient (1); some energy is also used to move limbs and is dissipated as heat (1).

question: Explain how Newton's Third Law relates to conservation of momentum. Use the example of two ice skaters pushing off each other to support your answer.
mark_scheme: Newton's Third Law: skater A pushes skater B with a force; B pushes A back with an equal and opposite force (1); forces act for the same time, so impulses are equal and opposite (1); impulse = change in momentum, so momentum changes are equal and opposite (1); total momentum before = 0; total momentum after = 0, so momentum is conserved (1).

question: A driver is travelling at 30 m/s on a motorway in wet conditions at night. Evaluate the factors that would affect the stopping distance compared to dry daytime conditions.
mark_scheme: Thinking distance affected by driver alertness / tiredness at night — may be longer (1); wet road reduces friction between tyres and road, increasing braking distance (1); higher speed greatly increases both thinking and braking distance (speed doubles, braking distance roughly quadruples) (1); any further factor: worn tyres, reduced visibility, vehicle load, tyre pressure (1).

question: A book rests on a table. Identify all forces acting on the book, state which are Newton's Third Law pairs, and explain why the book remains stationary.
mark_scheme: Weight of book acts downward (gravitational force from Earth) (1); normal contact force from table acts upward on book (1); Newton's Third Law pair: book's weight and the force the book exerts on the Earth (gravitational); normal force from table and force book exerts on table (1); book stationary because resultant force is zero — weight balanced by normal force (1).

question: A 0.5 kg ball hits a wall at 10 m/s and bounces back at 8 m/s. The impact lasts 0.02 s. Calculate the change in momentum and the average force exerted on the ball.
mark_scheme: Taking towards wall as positive: initial momentum = 0.5 × 10 = 5 kg m/s; final momentum = 0.5 × (−8) = −4 kg m/s (1); change in momentum = −4 − 5 = −9 kg m/s; magnitude = 9 kg m/s (1); F = Δp / t (1); F = 9 / 0.02 = 450 N (1).

question: A car of mass 900 kg is travelling at 20 m/s when the driver sees an obstacle and brakes to a halt. The braking force is 4500 N. Calculate the deceleration and stopping time from when brakes are applied. Then explain how airbags and seatbelts reduce injury during the stop.
mark_scheme: a = F / m = 4500 / 900 = 5 m/s² (deceleration) (1); t = (v − u) / a = (0 − 20) / (−5) = 4 s (1); airbags/seatbelts increase the time over which the passenger decelerates (1); same change in momentum spread over longer time means smaller force (F = Δp / t) (1); smaller force means less risk of serious injury to passenger (1).

question: Explain the difference between elastic and inelastic deformation. Describe how a force-extension graph shows both types. Calculate the spring constant if a force of 12 N produces an extension of 0.08 m, and calculate the elastic potential energy stored at this extension.
mark_scheme: Elastic deformation: object returns to original shape when force removed (1); inelastic (plastic) deformation: object does not return to original shape — permanently deformed (1); graph: straight line through origin = elastic region; curve beyond elastic limit = inelastic deformation (1); k = F / e = 12 / 0.08 = 150 N/m (1); Ee = ½ × 150 × (0.08)² = 0.48 J (1).

question: Describe how you would use a light gate and data logger to measure the acceleration of a trolley on a ramp. Include how you would process the data and what graph you would plot to determine the acceleration.
mark_scheme: Set up ramp with trolley; attach card of known length to trolley (1); light gate connected to data logger/timer measures velocity as card passes through (1); time how long card takes to cut beam; calculate velocity = card length / time (1); repeat at two points on ramp to get two velocities and the time between them; a = (v − u) / t (1); alternatively: plot velocity against time; gradient = acceleration (1).

question: A rocket of initial mass 20 000 kg (including 15 000 kg of fuel) produces a thrust of 250 000 N. Calculate the initial acceleration. Explain why the acceleration increases as fuel burns, even if the thrust remains constant.
mark_scheme: Weight = 20 000 × 10 = 200 000 N (1); resultant force = 250 000 − 200 000 = 50 000 N (1); a = F / m = 50 000 / 20 000 = 2.5 m/s² (1); as fuel burns, mass decreases (1); same thrust on smaller mass gives greater acceleration (F = ma, smaller m means larger a) (1).

question: A boat travels 30 m due north and then 40 m due east. Explain the difference between the distance travelled and the displacement. Calculate the magnitude of the final displacement and the angle from north.
mark_scheme: Distance = total path length = 30 + 40 = 70 m (1); displacement = straight-line distance from start to finish with direction (1); displacement magnitude = √(30² + 40²) = √(900 + 1600) = √2500 = 50 m (1); angle from north: tan θ = 40/30, θ = 53° east of north (accept 53° or correct calculation) (1); because displacement includes direction, it is a vector; distance is a scalar (1).

question: In a crash test, a 1200 kg car travelling at 15 m/s collides with a wall and stops in 0.3 s. Calculate the average braking force. Then evaluate the effectiveness of crumple zones, which extend the stopping time to 1.5 s in a real crash.
mark_scheme: Δp = m × Δv = 1200 × 15 = 18 000 kg m/s (1); F = Δp / t = 18 000 / 0.3 = 60 000 N without crumple zone (1); with crumple zone: F = 18 000 / 1.5 = 12 000 N (1); crumple zones reduce force by factor of 5 — significant reduction in risk of injury (1); same change in momentum but over longer time means much smaller force on occupants (1).

question: A parachutist falls from a stationary helicopter. Explain the motion of the parachutist from release to reaching terminal velocity, referring to resultant force, acceleration, and air resistance at each stage.
mark_scheme: At release, weight > air resistance so there is a downward resultant force (1); the parachutist accelerates downward (1); as speed increases, air resistance increases (1); resultant force decreases so acceleration decreases (1); eventually air resistance equals weight — resultant force zero — terminal velocity reached (constant speed, no acceleration) (1).

question: Describe the energy transfers when a ball is thrown upward and returns to its starting height. Explain why the ball's speed on return is slightly less than when thrown, and calculate the kinetic energy of a 0.3 kg ball thrown at 12 m/s.
mark_scheme: KE → GPE as ball rises (1); GPE → KE as ball falls (1); some energy dissipated as heat due to air resistance during both up and down journeys (1); therefore not all GPE converts back to KE — ball returns with less speed (1); KE = ½ mv² = ½ × 0.3 × 12² = ½ × 0.3 × 144 = 21.6 J (1).

question: Explain inertia and how it is related to mass. Describe how Newton's First Law links to inertia and give two everyday examples of inertia in action.
mark_scheme: Inertia is the tendency of an object to remain at rest or continue moving at constant velocity (1); greater mass = greater inertia (1); Newton's First Law: object stays at rest / constant velocity unless acted on by a resultant force — this is a statement of inertia (1); example 1: passengers lurch forward when car brakes suddenly — their bodies tend to continue moving (1); example 2: a heavy lorry is harder to stop than a bicycle at the same speed — greater mass means greater inertia (accept any valid examples) (1).

question: A train accelerates uniformly from 5 m/s to 35 m/s over 600 m. Calculate the acceleration and the time taken to cover this distance. Then calculate the distance the train would travel if it continued at 35 m/s for a further 2 minutes.
mark_scheme: v² = u² + 2as → (35)² = (5)² + 2 × a × 600 (1); 1225 − 25 = 1200a → a = 1 m/s² (1); t = (v − u) / a = (35 − 5) / 1 = 30 s (1); at constant 35 m/s for 2 min (120 s): d = v × t = 35 × 120 = 4200 m (1); allow full credit for any correct alternative method e.g. using area under graph (1 for correct formula, 1 for answer).

question: Explain the principle of conservation of momentum. A 4 kg trolley moving at 3 m/s collides with a 2 kg stationary trolley. After the collision the 4 kg trolley moves at 1 m/s in the same direction. Calculate the velocity of the 2 kg trolley after the collision and verify that momentum is conserved.
mark_scheme: Conservation of momentum: total momentum before a collision equals total momentum after, provided no external forces act (1); momentum before = (4 × 3) + (2 × 0) = 12 kg m/s (1); momentum after = (4 × 1) + (2 × v) = 4 + 2v (1); 4 + 2v = 12 → 2v = 8 → v = 4 m/s (1); momentum after = 4 + 8 = 12 kg m/s = momentum before — conservation verified (1).

question: A student investigates the motion of a ball rolled along a track. Sketch and describe the distance-time and velocity-time graphs for a ball that: rolls at constant speed, then accelerates, then decelerates to a stop. Explain what the gradient and area represent in each graph.
mark_scheme: Distance-time: constant speed = straight line with positive gradient (1); accelerating = upward curve (increasing gradient) (1); decelerating = curve flattening as gradient decreases to zero (1); gradient of distance-time graph = speed (1); velocity-time: constant speed = horizontal line; accelerating = straight line with positive gradient; decelerating = straight line with negative gradient (1); gradient of v-t graph = acceleration; area under v-t graph = distance travelled (1).

question: A logistics company is considering two lorries: Lorry A has mass 8000 kg and Lorry B has mass 12 000 kg, both with the same engine producing 60 000 N thrust. Friction on both is 20 000 N. Compare the performance of both lorries, calculating the acceleration of each and evaluating which is better suited to motorway driving versus urban stop-start driving.
mark_scheme: Resultant force = 60 000 − 20 000 = 40 000 N for both (1); acceleration A = 40 000 / 8000 = 5 m/s² (1); acceleration B = 40 000 / 12 000 = 3.3 m/s² (1); Lorry A has greater acceleration so better for urban driving where frequent starting and stopping required (1); Lorry B has greater mass so greater momentum at motorway speed — harder to stop but may carry more cargo (1); overall evaluation: Lorry A better for urban / Lorry B may be better for cargo capacity on motorway — with justification (1).

question: Explain Hooke's Law fully and describe the experiment to verify it. Include what measurements to take, what graph to plot, how to find the spring constant from the graph, and explain what happens when the elastic limit is exceeded.
mark_scheme: Hooke's Law: extension is proportional to force applied, provided elastic limit is not exceeded (1); add known masses (weights) to a spring; measure extension each time using a ruler (1); plot force (y-axis) against extension (x-axis); expect straight line through origin (1); spring constant k = gradient of the straight-line section (k = F/e) (1); beyond elastic limit, graph curves — extension greater than predicted by Hooke's Law (1); the spring undergoes inelastic/plastic deformation and does not return to original length when force is removed (1).

question: The Highway Code states that stopping distance at 30 mph is 23 m and at 60 mph is 73 m. Evaluate how thinking distance and braking distance each contribute to these totals, explain the physics behind why braking distance approximately quadruples when speed doubles, and discuss at least three factors that could make real-world stopping distances even longer.
mark_scheme: Thinking distance is proportional to speed — doubles when speed doubles (1); braking distance depends on kinetic energy: KE = ½mv² — when speed doubles, KE quadruples, so braking distance approximately quadruples (1); at 30 mph: thinking ≈ 9 m, braking ≈ 14 m; at 60 mph: thinking ≈ 18 m, braking ≈ 55 m — braking increases more than doubles (1); factor 1: driver distraction/tiredness increases reaction time and thinking distance (1); factor 2: wet/icy roads reduce friction, increasing braking distance (1); factor 3: worn tyres / brake fade / heavy vehicle load / downhill gradient (1).

question: Explain the difference between scalar and vector quantities. For a ship sailing 400 m north and then 300 m east, calculate the total distance travelled, the displacement magnitude and its direction. Explain why a navigator must use displacement rather than distance when plotting a course.
mark_scheme: Scalar: magnitude only (e.g. distance, speed, mass, temperature) (1); vector: magnitude and direction (e.g. displacement, velocity, force, acceleration) (1); total distance = 400 + 300 = 700 m (1); displacement = √(400² + 300²) = √(160 000 + 90 000) = √250 000 = 500 m (1); direction: tan θ = 300/400, θ = 36.9° ≈ 37° east of north (1); navigator needs displacement to know the actual straight-line distance and direction to destination — distance alone does not tell the direction (1).

question: A gun of mass 2 kg fires a bullet of mass 0.02 kg at 400 m/s. The gun and bullet were initially stationary. Calculate the recoil velocity of the gun. Explain this using conservation of momentum and Newton's Third Law. Then explain why the bullet causes more damage than the recoil force on the shooter, even though the forces are equal and opposite.
mark_scheme: Total initial momentum = 0 (both at rest) (1); conservation of momentum: 0 = (0.02 × 400) + (2 × v_gun) (1); 0 = 8 + 2v_gun → v_gun = −4 m/s; gun recoils at 4 m/s in opposite direction (1); Newton's Third Law: gun pushes bullet forward, bullet pushes gun backward with equal and opposite force (1); forces are equal but act on very different masses — bullet has tiny mass so enormous acceleration (a = F/m) (1); bullet has very high velocity and kinetic energy concentrated at a small point, causing much greater damage than the recoil force spread over the shooter's shoulder (1).

question: Evaluate the forces acting on an aeroplane in level flight at constant speed. The plane has mass 50 000 kg. Calculate its weight, identify all four forces acting on it, explain what must be true about the resultant force, and describe what happens to the forces and motion if the engine thrust is suddenly reduced by 20%.
mark_scheme: Weight = mg = 50 000 × 10 = 500 000 N downward (1); four forces: weight (down), lift (up), thrust (forward), drag (backward) (1); in level constant-speed flight: lift = weight AND thrust = drag — resultant force = zero (1); if thrust reduces by 20%: thrust < drag so resultant force backward — plane decelerates (1); also lift may reduce as airspeed decreases (1); pilot must increase thrust or adjust angle of attack to restore equilibrium or plane will slow down and potentially lose altitude (1).

question: Explain the relationship between work done, force, and distance. Calculate the work done pushing a 200 kg crate 15 m along a floor with a friction force of 400 N. Then explain how a ramp can make it easier to push the crate to a height of 2 m, comparing the force needed on the ramp versus lifting it vertically. (g = 10 N/kg)
mark_scheme: Work done = force × distance (in direction of force) (1); W = 400 × 15 = 6000 J along the floor (1); to lift vertically: F = weight = 200 × 10 = 2000 N; W = 2000 × 2 = 4000 J (1); ramp: same work done but over longer distance — so smaller force needed (work = force × distance; same W, larger d, smaller F) (1); this is the mechanical advantage of an inclined plane (1); however, using a ramp requires pushing through a greater distance — total work done is the same (ignoring friction) but effort force is less (1).

question: State two contact forces and two non-contact forces.
mark_scheme: Contact forces — any two: friction, normal contact force, tension, air resistance, upthrust (1); non-contact forces — any two: gravity, magnetic force, electrostatic force (1).

question: Give the definition of the resultant force acting on an object and state the unit.
mark_scheme: The resultant force is the single force that has the same effect as all the individual forces acting on an object combined (1); the unit is the newton (N) (1).

question: Name the quantity calculated by the equation M = F × d and state the unit.
mark_scheme: Moment (or turning moment or torque) (1); unit: newton-metre (N·m) (1).

question: Describe what is meant by pressure and state the equation for pressure in terms of force and area.
mark_scheme: Pressure is the force acting per unit area perpendicular to a surface (1); pressure = force ÷ area / P = F/A; unit is the pascal (Pa) (1).

question: State the equation for average speed and use it to calculate the speed of a car that travels 360 km in 4 hours.
mark_scheme: Speed = distance ÷ time (1); speed = 360 ÷ 4 = 90 km/h (1).

question: Give the equation that links force, mass and acceleration, and state what it is known as.
mark_scheme: F = ma (force = mass × acceleration) (1); Newton's second law of motion (1).

question: Describe what Newton's first law states about the motion of objects.
mark_scheme: An object will remain at rest or continue moving at a constant speed in a straight line (1); unless acted upon by a resultant (unbalanced) force (1).

question: State what is meant by weight and give the equation linking weight, mass and gravitational field strength.
mark_scheme: Weight is the force of gravity acting on an object (1); weight = mass × gravitational field strength / W = mg (1).

question: Give the principle of moments and state when a system is in equilibrium.
mark_scheme: The principle of moments states that for a system in equilibrium, the sum of clockwise moments equals the sum of anticlockwise moments (1); a system is in equilibrium when the resultant force and resultant moment about any point are both zero (1).

question: Describe what the gradient of a velocity-time graph represents and what the area under the graph represents.
mark_scheme: The gradient of a velocity-time graph represents acceleration (1); the area under the graph represents the distance (displacement) travelled (1).

question: Explain the difference between mass and weight. Include the units of each and explain why an astronaut's mass and weight are different on the Moon compared to on Earth.
mark_scheme: Mass is the amount of matter in an object — measured in kg, and does not change with location (1); weight is the gravitational force on an object — measured in newtons, depends on gravitational field strength (1); on the Moon g ≈ 1.6 N/kg compared to 10 N/kg on Earth — the astronaut's weight is about one-sixth, but mass is unchanged (1).

question: Describe what happens to the motion of an object when the resultant force acting on it is zero, is in the direction of motion, and is opposite to the direction of motion.
mark_scheme: Resultant force = zero: object stays at rest or moves at constant velocity (Newton's first law) (1); resultant force in direction of motion: object accelerates in that direction (1); resultant force opposite to direction of motion: object decelerates (negative acceleration) (1).

question: Explain how a lever works as a simple machine, using the concept of moments.
mark_scheme: A lever amplifies force by using the principle of moments: M = F × d (1); a small force applied at a large distance from the pivot produces the same moment as a large force at a small distance (1); example: a crowbar — applying a small force far from the pivot creates a large moment, enabling a large force to be applied to an object close to the pivot (1).

question: Describe how atmospheric pressure changes with altitude and explain this in terms of the air above.
mark_scheme: Atmospheric pressure decreases with increasing altitude (1); this is because at higher altitude there is less air above — the column of air exerting weight is shorter and has less mass (1); at sea level the full weight of the atmosphere acts; at higher altitudes, less atmosphere is above, so less force per unit area — lower pressure (1).

question: Explain Newton's third law and give an example with the two forces clearly identified.
mark_scheme: Newton's third law: when object A exerts a force on object B, object B exerts an equal and opposite force on object A (1); the forces are equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, and act on different objects (1); example: a book on a table — the book's weight acts downward on the table; the table exerts an equal normal contact force upward on the book (1).

question: Compare uniform acceleration and non-uniform acceleration. Describe how each would appear on a velocity-time graph.
mark_scheme: Uniform acceleration: acceleration is constant — velocity changes by the same amount each second (1); on a v-t graph: a straight line with a constant gradient (1); non-uniform acceleration: acceleration changes over time — on a v-t graph: a curved line whose gradient changes (1).

question: Explain the difference between thinking distance and braking distance and give one factor that affects each.
mark_scheme: Thinking distance: distance travelled while the driver reacts before brakes are applied — increases with speed; affected by reaction time (which increases with alcohol, tiredness or distractions) (1); braking distance: distance travelled after brakes are applied before the vehicle stops — affected by road conditions (wet/icy roads increase braking distance) and vehicle condition (worn brakes or tyres) (1); total stopping distance = thinking + braking distance (1).

question: Describe the forces acting on a skydiver at three stages: just after jumping, reaching terminal velocity, and after the parachute opens.
mark_scheme: Just after jumping: weight acts downward, air resistance is small — resultant force downward, skydiver accelerates (1); at terminal velocity: weight equals air resistance — resultant force is zero, constant speed (1); parachute opens: air resistance increases greatly — resultant force is upward, skydiver decelerates until new (lower) terminal velocity is reached (1).

question: Explain why a sharp knife cuts more easily than a blunt knife, using the concept of pressure.
mark_scheme: Pressure = force ÷ area (1); a sharp knife has a very small area at the cutting edge compared to a blunt knife (1); for the same applied force, the small area of the sharp blade produces a much greater pressure on the material being cut — enabling it to cut more easily (1).

question: Compare the forces and motion of a car travelling at constant speed with a car that is accelerating.
mark_scheme: Constant speed: driving force equals resistive forces (friction + air resistance) — resultant force is zero; velocity is constant by Newton's first law (1); accelerating: driving force is greater than resistive forces — there is a net forward resultant force (1); by Newton's second law (F = ma), the net force causes acceleration in the direction of the resultant force (1).

question: Explain how the position of the centre of mass of an object affects its stability.
mark_scheme: The centre of mass is the point where all the mass of an object can be considered to act (1); an object is stable if a vertical line through its centre of mass falls within its base — the weight creates a restoring moment if it is tilted (1); a lower centre of mass and/or a wider base increases stability — less likely to topple over when tilted (1).

question: Describe the motion of a ball thrown horizontally from a cliff top. Explain why its horizontal and vertical motions are independent.
mark_scheme: Horizontally: no horizontal force (ignoring air resistance) so horizontal velocity remains constant (1); vertically: gravity acts downward — the ball accelerates downward at g = 10 m/s², gaining vertical velocity over time (1); horizontal and vertical motions are independent because gravity only acts vertically — the ball's horizontal velocity is unaffected by gravitational acceleration (1).

question: State the equation linking acceleration, change in velocity and time.
mark_scheme: Acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time (a = Δv ÷ t) (1).

question: A car accelerates from 10 m/s to 30 m/s in 5 s. Calculate the acceleration of the car.
Explain the difference between acceleration and deceleration in terms of direction.
mark_scheme: Acceleration is a change in velocity in the direction of motion (1); deceleration is a negative acceleration — the change in velocity is opposite to the direction of motion (1).

question: Describe what a horizontal line on a velocity–time graph represents.
mark_scheme: A horizontal line represents constant velocity (1); the acceleration is zero (1).

question: A train decelerates uniformly from 50 m/s to rest in 25 s. Calculate the deceleration and the distance travelled during this time.
mark_scheme: a = Δv ÷ t = 50 ÷ 25 = 2 m/s² deceleration (1); distance = area under v–t graph = ½ × 50 × 25 (1); distance = 625 m (1).

question: A ball is dropped from rest and falls freely under gravity (g = 10 m/s²). Explain what happens to the velocity and acceleration of the ball as it falls, ignoring air resistance.
mark_scheme: The velocity increases as the ball accelerates downward (1); the acceleration remains constant at 10 m/s² throughout (1); this is because the only force acting is gravity, which is constant (1).

question: Use the equation v² = u² + 2as to calculate the final velocity of a car that accelerates at 3 m/s² over 48 m from rest.
State one example of a contact force.
mark_scheme: Any one from: friction; normal contact force; tension; air resistance (1).

question: State what is meant by the normal contact force.
mark_scheme: The normal contact force is the force exerted by a surface on an object perpendicular to the surface (1).

question: Explain why friction is considered a contact force.
mark_scheme: Friction acts between two surfaces that are in contact (1); it opposes relative motion between the surfaces (1).

question: A book rests on a table. Explain the forces acting on the book in terms of Newton's laws.
mark_scheme: Gravity acts downward on the book (1); the table exerts an equal and opposite normal contact force upward on the book, so it is in equilibrium (1).

question: Compare friction and air resistance as contact forces.
mark_scheme: Both are contact forces that oppose motion (1); friction acts between solid surfaces in contact, while air resistance acts between a moving object and the air (a fluid) (1).

question: Describe how the force of friction between two surfaces can be increased.
mark_scheme: Increase the roughness of one or both surfaces (1); increase the normal contact force / weight pressing the surfaces together (1); [award 3rd mark for] use of a material with higher coefficient of friction, e.g. rubber instead of ice (1).

question: A car travels at constant speed on a straight, level road. Explain the contact forces involved.
mark_scheme: The driving force from the engine acts forward (1); friction/air resistance acts backward opposing motion (1); because the car is at constant speed these forces are balanced / resultant force is zero (1).

question: State what is meant by a resultant force.
mark_scheme: The resultant force is the single force that has the same effect as all the individual forces acting on an object combined (1).

question: State what happens to an object when the resultant force acting on it is zero.
mark_scheme: The object remains stationary or continues to move at constant velocity (in a straight line) (1).

question: Two horizontal forces act on an object: 15 N to the right and 6 N to the left. Calculate the resultant force and state its direction.
mark_scheme: Resultant = 15 − 6 = 9 N (1); direction: to the right (1).

question: Explain what it means for an object to be in equilibrium.
mark_scheme: The resultant force on the object is zero (1); so the object is either stationary or moving at constant velocity (1).

question: Describe how to find the resultant of two forces acting at right angles using a scale drawing.
mark_scheme: Draw the two forces as arrows to scale at right angles (1); draw the diagonal of the rectangle / complete the parallelogram — the diagonal represents the resultant (magnitude and direction) (1).

question: An object has three forces acting on it: 10 N upward, 4 N downward, and 3 N to the right. Calculate the resultant vertical force and state whether the object accelerates vertically.
mark_scheme: Vertical resultant = 10 − 4 = 6 N upward (1); since the resultant force is not zero the object accelerates vertically (1); the horizontal 3 N force does not affect vertical motion (1).

question: A skydiver jumps from a plane. Describe how the resultant force changes from the moment they jump until they reach terminal velocity.
mark_scheme: At the start, weight > air resistance so there is a net downward resultant force and the skydiver accelerates (1); as speed increases, air resistance increases, reducing the resultant force (1); at terminal velocity, air resistance = weight, resultant force = 0 and acceleration = 0 (1).

question: State the equation linking pressure, force and area.
mark_scheme: Pressure = force ÷ area (P = F ÷ A) (1).

question: State the unit of pressure.
mark_scheme: Pascal (Pa) (1). [Accept N/m².]

question: A force of 200 N acts on an area of 0.04 m². Calculate the pressure exerted.
Explain why a drawing pin can be pushed into a board more easily than a finger pressing on the board.
mark_scheme: The drawing pin has a very small area at the point (1); so for the same force, the pressure at the tip is much greater (1).

question: Explain how pressure in a liquid changes with depth.
mark_scheme: Pressure increases with depth (1); because the weight of liquid above increases with depth, creating greater pressure (1).

question: A rectangular block has a base area of 0.05 m² and exerts a pressure of 4000 Pa on a surface. Calculate the weight of the block.
Explain why a hydraulic system can be used to multiply a force, referring to pressure.
mark_scheme: Pressure is transmitted equally throughout a liquid (1); a small force applied over a small area creates a pressure (1); the same pressure acting over a larger area on the output piston produces a larger force (1).

question: State the equation linking speed, distance and time.
mark_scheme: Speed = distance ÷ time (1).

question: State the difference between speed and velocity.
mark_scheme: Velocity is speed in a specified direction / velocity is a vector, speed is a scalar (1).

question: A cyclist travels 360 m in 45 s. Calculate the average speed of the cyclist.
mark_scheme: Speed = distance ÷ time = 360 ÷ 45 (1); speed = 8 m/s (1).

question: Describe how to calculate the average speed of an object from a distance–time graph.
mark_scheme: Calculate the gradient of the graph (1); gradient = change in distance ÷ change in time = average speed (1).

question: Explain what a straight line on a distance–time graph tells you about the motion of an object.
mark_scheme: A straight line indicates constant speed (1); the steeper the gradient, the greater the speed (1).

question: A car travels at 30 m/s. Convert this speed to km/h and determine how far the car travels in 2.5 hours.
mark_scheme: 30 m/s × 3600 ÷ 1000 = 108 km/h (1); distance = speed × time = 108 × 2.5 (1); distance = 270 km (1).

question: A distance–time graph shows a curved line with increasing gradient. Describe and explain the motion shown.
mark_scheme: The object is accelerating (1); the gradient (speed) is increasing over time (1); the curve shows non-uniform / changing speed rather than constant speed (1).

question: Explain the difference between elastic and inelastic deformation of a spring.
mark_scheme: Elastic deformation means the spring returns to its original shape when the force is removed (1); inelastic (plastic) deformation means the spring is permanently deformed and does not return to its original shape (1).

question: State one example of a non-contact force.
mark_scheme: Any one from: gravity / gravitational force; magnetic force; electrostatic force (1).

question: Explain the difference between a contact force and a non-contact force, giving one example of each.
mark_scheme: A contact force requires physical contact between objects, e.g. friction / normal force (1); a non-contact force acts at a distance without physical contact, e.g. gravity / magnetism (1).

question: State the equation for calculating the moment of a force.
mark_scheme: Moment = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot (1).

question: State the unit of moment.
mark_scheme: Newton-metre (N m) (1).

question: A force of 40 N is applied at a perpendicular distance of 0.5 m from a pivot. Calculate the moment of the force.
mark_scheme: Moment = force × distance = 40 × 0.5 (1); moment = 20 N m (1).

question: State the principle of moments and explain how it applies to a balanced see-saw.
mark_scheme: The principle of moments states that for a body in equilibrium the sum of clockwise moments equals the sum of anticlockwise moments (1); on a balanced see-saw, the clockwise moment equals the anticlockwise moment about the pivot (1).

question: A uniform beam is balanced on a pivot at its centre. A 30 N force acts 2 m to the left of the pivot. Calculate the force needed 1.5 m to the right of the pivot to balance the beam.
mark_scheme: Anticlockwise moment = 30 × 2 = 60 N m (1); for balance, clockwise moment = 60 N m (1); F = 60 ÷ 1.5 = 40 N (1).

question: Explain why it is easier to open a door by pushing at the edge furthest from the hinge than near the hinge.
mark_scheme: The moment (turning effect) depends on both force and perpendicular distance from the pivot (hinge) (1); pushing at the edge gives the maximum perpendicular distance (1); so a smaller force is needed to produce the same moment (1).

question: State the difference between a scalar and a vector quantity.
mark_scheme: A scalar has magnitude only; a vector has both magnitude and direction (1).

question: Classify each of the following as scalar or vector: speed, velocity, mass, force, temperature.
mark_scheme: Scalars: speed, mass, temperature (1); vectors: velocity, force (1).

question: Explain why displacement is a vector quantity but distance is a scalar.
mark_scheme: Displacement specifies both how far and in which direction from a reference point (1); distance only gives the total path length with no direction information (1).

question: State the two distances that make up the total stopping distance of a vehicle.
mark_scheme: Thinking distance and braking distance (1).

question: Explain how tiredness affects the stopping distance of a car.
mark_scheme: Tiredness increases reaction time (1); which increases thinking distance / the distance travelled before the brakes are applied (1).

question: State the equation linking work done, force and distance.
mark_scheme: Work done = force × distance moved in the direction of the force (W = F × d) (1).

question: State the unit of work done.
mark_scheme: Joule (J) (1).

question: A person pushes a box with a force of 25 N over a distance of 8 m. Calculate the work done on the box.
Explain why no work is done on a book resting on a shelf.
mark_scheme: Work is only done when a force causes displacement in the direction of the force (1); the book is stationary so there is no displacement — no work is done (1).

question: A crane lifts a 500 kg steel beam to a height of 12 m. Calculate the work done against gravity. (g = 10 N/kg)
